title: A giant built just like you
hook: Make a person 10 times bigger, same shape, same bone. Are the legs still up to the job?

doesNotKnow: that weight grows with the cube of size but bone cross-section only with the square
so each square centimetre of bone in a scaled-up body carries more load in proportion to its size

misconception: A giant built exactly like a person, just 10 times larger, would be just as sturdy.
objective: The learner can explain that scaling every length by 10 multiplies weight by 1,000 but bone cross-section by only 100, so load per square centimetre rises 10 times; that much thicker bones would keep it level; and that real large mammals mostly keep bone stress level by posture instead.

claims.text: Scaling every length by k multiplies weight (volume, same material) by k³ and bone cross-section by k², so the load on each square centimetre of bone grows by k: at 10×, weight ×1,000, bone area ×100, load ×10.
claims.source: Geometry of similar solids (prerequisites math:area-scaling, math:volume-scaling); company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs #3; Demo.tsx scaleOf(). Static axial load only; the model ignores bending and dynamic loads.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation: similar solids scaled by k have volume x k^3 (so weight x k^3 at the same density) and every area x k^2, so load per unit bone area = k^3 / k^2 = k. Node: k = 10 gives 1,000 / 100 = 10; Demo.tsx scaleOf(10, false) gives the same, and the reveal prints them. The recall's statue (k = 3: 27 / 9 = 3) is the same derivation. The model is static axial load only; the claim says so.

claims.text: Galileo argued in 1638 that giants need disproportionately thick bones.
claims.source: Galilei, G. (1638), Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (Two New Sciences), Second Day (public domain; the bone figure and passage on giants, section to confirm). Not opened by the builder.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD (class P). Galileo 1638, Two New Sciences, Second Day, could not be opened: no public-domain copy is reachable from this host (Gutenberg, archive.org and Wikisource blocked; no OpenStax text discusses it). Not verified on trust. The lesson does not need it: the 'thicker legs' result is c1/c4 derivation. If W-583 cannot open it, cut the Galileo sentence (cm-big-ideas-science's call). | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Learner text (Demo.tsx line 68): 'Galileo argued in 1638 that giants need disproportionately thick bones.' Opened on PMC. Sci Adv 2019 5(1): eaat4269, 'Scaling of bird wings and feathers for efficient flight' (PMC6357743): 'Galileo Galilei was one of the first scientists to discuss scaling trends in nature, observing that a scaled-up giant ten times taller than ordinary man could not exist in the natural world unless his limbs were greatly altered to bear the extra mass (1)', with ref. 1 Galilei, Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences. Hutchinson 2021, J Exp Biol 224: jeb217463 (PMC8214834), dates the work: scaling of the limb skeleton was 'inspired by Galileo's (1638) original insights', with the reference 'Galileo, G. (1638). Two New Sciences'. Together they support the year, the giant and the need for disproportionately strengthened limb bones. Galileo's text itself is not opened (no public-domain copy on an allow-listed host).

claims.text: Where it stops: big mammals mostly stand more upright instead of growing far thicker bones, which keeps peak bone stress roughly level across sizes.
claims.source: Biewener, A. A. (1989), 'Scaling body support in mammals: limb posture and muscle mechanics', Science 245(4913), 45-48: bone allometry is modest; larger mammals reduce peak stresses mainly through more upright limbs (better mechanical advantage). Holds roughly up to horse size; the largest mammals (elephants) are also slower and less athletic (to confirm). The lesson's one held citation (class H) on the learner path; Galileo (c2, 1638) is public domain (class P). Not opened by the builder. Cut if not checkable; fallback (v2, W-634): the reveal's last paragraph becomes 'Where it stops: real animals change shape and posture as they grow.' (support: convention, illustrated by the stage's 'thicker legs' toggle, c4), with no claim about bone stress in mammals.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD (the lesson's one class-H citation). Biewener 1989 (Science 245) could not be opened (web blocked), and no openable source covers limb posture and bone stress scaling. Not verified on trust. The v2 fallback is ready and verifiable as convention: 'Where it stops: real animals change shape and posture as they grow.' Use it if W-583 cannot open Biewener. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Learner text (Demo.tsx line 70): 'Where it stops: big mammals mostly stand more upright instead of growing far thicker bones, which keeps bone stress ...'. Opened on PMC: 'Where Have All the Giants Gone? How Animals Deal with the Problem of Size', PLoS Biol 2017 15(1): e2000473 (PMC5226675). It says 'changes in bone properties or changes in bone shape do not fully counteract the size-related increases in stress', that 'larger animals move with an upright posture and extended joints', and that 'By adopting a more upright posture, large animals are able to increase the effective mechanical advantage (EMA) ... and consequently decrease musculoskeletal stress ... EMA has been shown to scale with M^0.25, which nearly matches the predicted increase in stress that would occur if posture did not change'. Hutchinson 2021, J Exp Biol 224: jeb217463 (PMC8214834): 'minimal long bone circumference tends to scale isometrically versus body mass – or at most with weak positive allometry', and peak tissue stresses are 'maintained within safe bounds' (Biewener 1989). Biewener 1989 itself is not opened; these two reviews are the basis.

claims.text: The limit line (4× today's load) and the thicker-legs model (bone diameter ×k^1.5, so load stays level) are the lesson's illustrations, not measured values.
claims.source: Labelled 'limit (illustrative)' on the stage. 4× is chosen to sit within the 2-4 safety factors reported for limb bones in vigorous activity (Biewener, A. A. (1990), 'Biomechanics of mammalian terrestrial locomotion', Science 250(4984), 1097-1103; to confirm). Thicker legs: diameter ∝ k^1.5 gives cross-section ∝ k³ = weight, so load ×1 (derivation).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Convention: LIMIT = 4 in Demo.tsx, and the stage labels the line 'limit (illustrative)'; the reveal calls it 'the illustrative limit'. Thicker legs: diameter x k^1.5 gives area x k^3, load x 1 (node: 1 at k = 2, 3, 5, 10). The reason given for 4x (Biewener 1990 safety factors of 2 to 4) is not on the learner path and was not checked; it does not affect this verdict.

claims.text: With same-shape legs, each square centimetre of bone in the 10× giant carries more than the illustrative limit.
claims.source: 10 > 4 (c1, c4). The stage colours the legs and the bar red above the line. The lesson does not claim a 10× giant would collapse standing still: real standing stresses are far below bone strength, and the margin that disappears is the one used in running and jumping (c4).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation: 10 > 4 (c1, c4), and the code turns legs and bar red when load > LIMIT. The lesson makes no collapse claim, so nothing here rests on real bone strength.

recall.question: A statue is copied at 3 times the size in every direction, in the same stone. Compared with the original, the pressure on the stone at its base is about…
recall.why: Weight grows 27 times (3³) but the base area only 9 times (3²), so the pressure on each bit of base grows 3 times, the scale factor itself.
